Aspiration or Injection
Aspiration may be a helpful adjunct in the diagnosis and management of a ganglion or synovial
cyst.
Steroid injections in an arthritic knee may help with the symptoms associated with a Baker
cyst.
Sclerotherapy, the injection of a caustic substance, may be an important tool in the
management of vascular lesions.
Radiation Therapy
Radiation therapy can be used as part of a multidisciplinary approach to the management of
desmoid tumors1-4 and tenosynovial giant cell tumors.5,6
Radiation therapy plays little role in the management of other benign tumors (Resource 2).
Systemic Therapy
Systemic therapy options are available for the management of tenosynovial giant cell
tumors/pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS),7,8 fibromatosis/desmoid tumors,9-11 and
neurofibromas.12,13
These therapies should be used as part of a multidisciplinary approach.
Surgical Management
Surgical management may include biopsy or excision.
Arthroscopy is a valuable treatment option for benign intra-articular tumors.
If diagnosis of a mass is in question, biopsy or excision should be performed at an institution
that provides multidisciplinary sarcoma care.

Universal Surgical Approach
Most benign soft-tissue tumors can be removed with a marginal margin.
A wide margin is reserved for malignant tumors or those with a high potential for local
recurrence.
Sarcomas
Desmoid fibromatosis
Arthroscopic procedures should not be used in the treatment of patients in whom malignancy
is suspected.
Surgeons should plan for the possibility of a change in diagnosis and the need for secondary
surgery with wide margins.
Incision location that may be extended for secondary surgery
Longitudinal incisions in line with the anatomic compartment
Incision centered over the mass
Limit dissection to necessary planes and avoid unnecessary exploration of critical
neurovascular structures.
Narrow suture lines

Unique Surgical and Treatment Considerations
Cystic Soft-Tissue Lesions
Benign cystic soft-tissue masses are a diverse group of neoplastic and non-neoplastic entities.
The appropriate treatment option depends on the underlying pathology and biologic behavior
of the process process (Resource 3).
Popliteal (Baker) Synovial Cyst
A distension of the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa (Figure 1)
Can occur in children; most common after age 50 years.
Most often is a secondary manifestation of intra-articular pathology.
Reassurance and education are key aspects of management.
Management is directed at the underlying joint pathology
Intra-articular injection
Arthroscopic management of intra-articular pathology

May be considered if cyst is causing neurovascular compromise
Should be performed in combination with management of intra-articular knee pathology

Popliteal (Baker) Synovial Cyst
Reassurance and patient education are important aspects of the management of
popliteal cysts. Education centers on informing patients that treatment should not be
focused on removal of the cyst. In most patients, management of the underlying joint
pathology will result in the relief of symptoms related to the cyst.14
If cyst excision is performed, open and arthroscopic techniques can be successful. In
2016, Saylik et al15 reported a 2% recurrence rate after arthroscopic management of
underlying joint pathology in combination with open cyst removal. Techniques for
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Surgical Management of Benign Soft-Tissue Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000563
4/27

successful arthroscopic management of popliteal cysts also have been described.16-18 In
2018, Brazier et al19 described a technique that involves the use of anteromedial,
anterolateral, posteromedial and occasional transcystic portals. This technique focuses
on takedown of the posterior transverse synovial infold, a valve-type structure
implicated in the one-way flow of synovial fluid into the cysts. This resulted in a
substantial decrease in the size of all cysts and improved clinical outcomes in 94% of
patients.
Acromioclavicular Cyst
Secondary to underlying acromioclavicular joint or rotator cuff pathology
Simple excision is not indicated.
Aspiration is associated with a high recurrence rate.
Injections directed at the underlying pathology may be beneficial.
Surgical management is directed at the underlying pathology.
Wrist Ganglia
Present in more than one-half of asymptomatic individuals
May be volar or dorsal
Observation is reasonable given a high rate of spontaneous resolution.
Management
Aspiration may provide relief of symptoms.
Steroid injections do not decrease recurrence rates.
Open surgical excision
Arthroscopic surgical excision

Wrist Ganglia
Wrist ganglia are very common in the general population and often are not associated
with any functional problems. A patient’s request for treatment often is for cosmesis or
concern of malignancy. Surgeons must consider other diagnoses, such as tumors,
including malignancies, which can masquerade as a ganglion cyst. Reassurance and

education may be adequate treatment options because as many as 42% of volar and
dorsal ganglion cysts have been shown to spontaneously resolve.20 Recurrence rates
after open surgical removal vary greatly. Arthroscopic cyst removal techniques are
associated with recurrence and complication rates similar to those of open techniques.
Intraneural Ganglia
Likely represent intraneural tracking of a degenerative cyst of an adjacent joint
Most commonly observed in the common peroneal nerve associated with an articular branch
of the proximal tibiofibular joint21
Surgical management should include addressing the joint pathology and/or transecting the
articular branch of the associated nerve (Figure 2).

If concern for a malignant nerve tumor exists, then biopsy should be performed by a

Schwannoma
Schwannomas represent approximately 5% of benign soft-tissue tumors. The diagnosis
often is strongly suggested by the clinical presentation and imaging characteristics. Many
patients will describe sharp, electrical-like pain and have a positive Tinel sign in the
distribution of the affected nerve. If the diagnosis is in doubt, then a biopsy can be
performed following the same surgical techniques as those used for excision of the
mass.
A schwannoma is contained within the epineurium and predominantly displaces the
adjacent nerve fascicles. The goal of surgical management is to open the epineurium

longitudinally in an area where there are no significant nerve fibers between the
epineurium and the tumor. This incision is made through the onion skin–like epineurium
until the shiny surface of the tumor is encountered. After this incision is made, the
schwannoma often can be enucleated from the nerve. Visual magnification with the use
of surgical loupes or a microscope aids in identification of the traversing nerve fascicles.
Although not proven to decrease complication rates, the use of nerve stimulators or
neural monitoring may help identify the location of functional motor nerve fascicles
intraoperatively22 (Figure 5).
Figure 5
Clinical photograph shows the characteristic appearance of an excised schwannoma.
(Courtesy of Jeremy White, MD, Oklahoma City, OK.)

Schwannomas commonly are thought to be able to be removed without loss of
neurologic function; however, many studies report common transient neurologic deficits
ranging from 10%23 to 76%.24 Although many of the lasting effects are minor, the risk of
some permanent neurologic deficit has been reported to be as high as 36%,24 with
permanent decrease in motor function reported in approximately 10% of patients.25 The
patient should be educated about the high risk of transient neurologic deficits and the
low risk of substantial permanent neurologic deficits.
Malignant transformation is rare, and local recurrence rates are low, even with
piecemeal or incomplete excision.22 In major peripheral nerves, preference should be
given to protection of the associated nerve rather than complete tumor excision
(Resource 4).
Neurofibroma
10% are associated with neurofibromatosis 1
Variable growth pattern, which influences treatment options
Localized intraneural neurofibroma
Localized cutaneous neurofibroma
Diffuse infiltrative neurofibroma
Plexiform neurofibroma
Surgical treatment principles
Marginal excision is appropriate for localized cutaneous neurofibromas and localized
intraneural tumors in expendable nerves.
The infiltrative growth pattern makes excision of intraneural neurofibromas associated with
major peripheral nerves difficult without damage to the underlying nerve.
The same surgical principles that are applied to schwannomas are used in the management
of neurofibromas.
Perform surgical management under loupe or microscope magnification.
Identify and protect major nerve fascicles intraoperatively.
Piecemeal excision is acceptable in major peripheral nerves to save function.

Neurofibroma
Neurofibromas represent approximately 5% of benign soft-tissue tumors. Although
cutaneous neurofibromas simply can be marginally excised, the invasive growth pattern
of neurofibromas makes surgical removal from major peripheral nerves a challenge.
Despite this challenge, successful, safe removal of localized intraneural neurofibromas
from major peripheral nerves has been reported.25
Nonsurgical treatment modalities that can be effective for neurofibromas include
antihistamines, antifibrotic agents, anti-angiogenesis agents, hormone therapy, Ras
protein mediators, and interferon alpha. These nonsurgical treatment modalities for
neurofibromas should be explored with a multidisciplinary team if surgical management
would result in a high risk for complications.
Intra-articular/Synovial Tumors
Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor
Proliferative disorder of the synovium characterized by hemosiderin deposition and
inflammation
PVNS and giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath (GCTTS) are two variants of tenosynovial giant
cell tumors representing a single pathologic entity, with the name varying based location.
GCTTS occurs as a distinct peritendinous nodule.
PVNS occurs inside a joint in two distinct forms.
Nodular/localized
Diffuse
Treatment options
Observation may be appropriate in patient with minimal or no symptoms.
Radiation therapy may be considered for refractory disease.
Pexidartinib has been approved by the FDA for patients in whom surgical treatment is
associated with a high risk for morbidity.
Surgical management is the mainstay of treatment.

Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor
Tenosynovial giant cell tumors represent a proliferative disorder of the synovium
characterized by inflammation and hemosiderin deposition. If they occur along a
tendon, tenosynovial giant cell tumors are referred to as GCTTS. Tenosynovial giant
cell tumors in an intra-articular location are referred to as PVNS; however, these
conditions encompass a single pathologic entity. The mainstay of management is
surgical excision. In patients with the nodular form, such as GCTTS, or
nodular/localized PVNS, removal can be achieved in a straightforward manner via
marginal excision. In such instances, a lower rate of recurrence may be expected, and
avoiding piecemeal excision of nodular lesions has been reported to minimize the
rate of recurrence.2 In patients with diffuse PVNS, surgical treatment may be a
challenge, resulting in recurrences rates ranging from 8% to 44%.2,26 An arthroscopic
or open approach, or occasionally a combination of the two approaches, may be used
for the surgical management of diffuse PVNS. Anterior and posterior approaches to
the involved joint (often the knee) may be necessary to débride all abnormal tissue. If
performed arthroscopically, specialized posterior portals may be necessary, and 30°
and 70° arthroscopes should be available. Studies have described complete
synovectomy as a method to reduce the risk of recurrence.27 An open approach to
the posterior aspect of the knee places the crucial neurovascular structures of the
popliteal space at risk, and consideration should be given to referral to a surgeon
familiar with this approach.
Radiation therapy may be considered in patents with refractory disease. The role of
radiation therapy generally is limited to multiply recurrent lesions that have been
unresponsive to surgical management; although radiation therapy has also been used
in combination with surgical management.5,6,13,28,29 External beam radiation therapy
and intra-articular radionuclide injection (Y-90) may be used. Radiation therapy may
result in considerable adverse effects, including fibrosis, tissue necrosis, skin changes,
and secondary malignancy. Recently, promising developments have been made in the
medical management of tenosynovial giant cell tumors. Overexpression of colony
stimulating factor 1 is thought to contribute to the abnormal proliferative process.

Pexidartinib is an oral agent and colony stimulating factor-1 inhibitor. Pexidartinib has
resulted in a 39% response rate in the management of these tumors;30 however, a
13% rate of considerable adverse events has been reported, with hair color change
being the most common adverse event and hepatotoxicity being the most severe
adverse event (Resource 5).
Synovial Chondromatosis
A portion of the synovium undergoes metaplasia and produces cartilaginous nodules.
The nodules can detach, becoming loose bodies in the joint that can undergo calcification or
ossification (Figure 7).
Management: arthroscopic removal of symptomatic loose bodies with synovectomy aimed at
excision of metastatic synovium
Figure 7
Clinical photograph shows multiple loose bodies excised from an ankle with diffuse synovial
chondromatosis. (Courtesy of David Greenberg, MD, St. Louis, MO.)

Synovial Chondromatosis
Synovial chondromatosis is a benign intra-articular process, most commonly
occurring in the knee, in which a portion of the synovial lining undergoes metaplastic
transformation and begins producing cartilage nodules rather than normal synovial
fluid. This may result in a very large volume of loose bodies. The goal of management

14/27

involves mitigating symptoms by removing the loose bodies and attempting to isolate
the region of synovial metaplasia to facilitate excision and thereby decrease the rate
of recurrence rate. This usually is best accomplished via an arthroscopic approach,
which affords enhanced visualization and is associated with decreased morbidity
compared with an open approach.31,32 In many patients, the region of cartilage
metaplasia may be a challenge to locate, and a more extensive synovectomy may be
necessary, especially in patients with recurrent disease, to minimize the risk of
additional recurrence. Occasionally, the nodules can become quite large and push
into extra-articular locations. Similarly, the synovial lining of tendon sheaths can
undergo similar metaplasia, resulting in extra-articular deposits of cartilaginous
bodies. In such instances, an open approach to management is required but likely will
result in increased morbidity compared with arthroscopic management33 (Resource
6).
Lipoma Arborescens
A diffuse proliferative process of the synovium characterized by the replacement of sub-
synovial tissue with adipocytes.
Etiology unknown but likely is a reaction to chronic inflammation.
Surgical management via open and arthroscopic methods has been described,
Recurrence is rare.

Lipoma arborescens
Lipoma arborescens is a benign proliferation of adipocytes replacing the sub-synovial
tissue in a diffuse manner, resulting in frond-like villous projections. Lipoma arborescens
often is noted incidentally on imaging studies obtained for other indications; in such
instances, lipoma arborescens can be safely observed. Lipoma arborescens also may be
associated with persistent knee swelling and achiness; in such instances, open or
arthroscopic excision may be considered. Historically, open synovectomy and mass
removal have been the preferred treatment options, resulting in low rates of recurrence.

MRI findings overlap enough with those of soft-tissue sarcomas that a biopsy is required for

Although historically managed surgically, recent recommendations have centered on active

In 2020, the Desmoid Tumor Working Group developed the algorithm for the management of
desmoid tumors shown in Figure 8.

Desmoid Tumors/Fibromatosis
Extra-abdominal desmoid tumors, or fibromatosis, are a locally aggressive process that
does not respect anatomic boundaries and may involve critical neurovascular structures.
Desmoid tumors are associated with an unpredictable growth pattern, and some tumors
may stabilize or even regress. Historically, the cornerstone of management has been
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:45 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of Benign Soft-Tissue Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000563
17/27

resection with wide margins; however, because of the extensive and infiltrative nature of
these tumors, surgical management may be associated with considerable morbidity.
Even with wide margins, local recurrence is very common. Event-free survival after
surgical management may be equivalent to that of active observation only.35
Recent treatment recommendations have centered on initial observation of newly
diagnosed lesions. In 2020, the Desmoid Tumor Working Group developed a treatment
algorithm for the management of desmoid tumors that recommends active surveillance
as the front-line approach. Active surveillance is outlined as continuous patient
monitoring, with the first follow-up MRI obtained within 1 to 2 months, followed by
follow-up MRI at 3 to 6 months. A decision with regard to active management should be
postponed until progression is identified at two to three subsequent follow-up intervals,
possibly not within the first year. A decision with regard to active management can be
accelerated if progression is predicted to result in a considerable increase in morbidity. If
active management is pursued, the Desmoid Tumor Working Group recommends
considering medical management unless surgical management is associated with a low
risk of morbidity. Radiation therapy and isolated limb perfusion are additional treatment
options for desmoid tumors in the extremity.11
Medical therapy options for desmoid tumors include hormone treatment, NSAIDs,
tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and low-dose or conventional chemotherapy agents. Such
medical management should be supervised by a multidisciplinary group at an institution
with experience managing desmoid tumors (Resource 8).

Vascular Lesions
Benign vascular tumors present along a broad spectrum ranging from cutaneous
hemangiomas to large, deep vascular malformations. Orthopaedic surgeons may
encounter these deep vascular malformations with some regularity because they often
occur in the muscles of the extremities; therefore, they also have been referred to as
intramuscular hemangiomas. These tumors are composed of broad nests of abnormal
capillaries interdigitating with normal tissue and may be quite extensive. Therefore, they
can present a considerable management challenge. Fortunately, they generally are
distinguishable on imaging studies, with radiographs demonstrating phleboliths and
MRIs revealing characteristic vascular channels. The administration of contrast aids in
this distinction. If the diagnosis is certain, most benign vascular tumors can be managed
symptomatically and often respond to treatment options such as aspirin and
compression. For lesions that in which nonsurgical treatment options have been
exhausted and the patient remains substantially symptomatic, management may be
considered. These lesions often are amenable to interventional radiology techniques,
such as sclerotherapy. For lesions that are not successfully managed via interventional
techniques, surgical management may be considered. Because involvement of normal
tissues often is extensive, the surgeon should carefully consider treatment advantages
versus morbidity and the extent of surgical management. The patient should be
extensively counseled on the level of current symptoms versus postoperative
expectations to verify the potential for surgical advantages. Similarly, the patient should
be counseled on the extremely high rate of recurrence, with some studies reporting
rates as high as 38%.44 Technically, these surgical procedures may be very challenging
given the interdigitation with normal tissues, difficulty locating the mass because of its
usually nonpalpable nature, and difficulty differentiating normal tissue from lesional
tissue. The goal is to identify and disrupt feeding vessels a while removing all abnormal
vascular tissue without compromising any crucial nearby structures, such as
neurovascular elements.

A solitary fibrous tumor is a somewhat poorly understood tumor of vascular origin that
previously was called hemangioendothelioma. It may exhibit benign and malignant
behavior. Therefore, solitary fibrous tumors that are encountered should be referred to
a surgeon who specializes in management of soft-tissue malignancies. In most patients,
wide excision is appropriate (Resource 9).

Atypical Lipomatous Tumors
If a lesion appears consistent with fat on all MRI sequences, then biopsy tends to not aid
in treatment decisions. In such situations, the differential diagnosis includes a lipoma
and an atypical lipomatous tumor. Both entities are appropriately managed via marginal
resection. Radiation therapy is not indicated in the management of atypical lipomatous
tumors. Atypical lipomatous tumors are associated with a higher risk of recurrence than
lipomas (10% to 50%) and a very low risk of malignant transformation; therefore, they
should be followed via surveillance MRI for 2 years.45-47 Symptomatic reevaluation can
be performed after that time (Resource 10).
